summary.title: Gamedev on Ruby? Why not!
summary.one_liner: You learn how to build a terminal Snake game in Ruby, structured as board, snake, food and game classes, each driven by RSpec tests.
keywords: ruby array object_id block vs array.new
takeaways: Structure a small Ruby game into Board, Snake, Food and Game classes with a lib/ and spec/ layout.
Represent the snake as an array of [x, y] coordinates, moving it by unshifting a new head and popping the tail.
Use a custom AteItselfError to end the game when the snake collides with itself, and wrap the board so the snake wraps at walls.
Avoid shared-reference bugs by building 2D arrays with a block (Array.new(n){ Array.new(m, '.') }) rather than Array.new(n, Array.new(m)).
Read keypresses without blocking the render loop, using a GetKey helper module described in the article.
summary.summary: The article walks through building a terminal Snake game in Ruby (tested with RSpec and debugged with Pry), using a folder layout with lib/ and spec/ directories. It goes component by component: a Board class that creates a grid filled with dots, a Snake class modeled as an array of coordinate parts with turn, step, and increase methods, a Food class placed at random, and a Game class that runs a tick loop, checks collisions, and handles key input. Code snippets for each spec and class are shown alongside explanations, and the author notes a block-vs-shared-reference array pitfall. The conclusion suggests extensions such as walls, two-player mode, or enemies. The article states it was written against Ruby 2.3.1.
